title: Persecution is God's testing, not the devil's work
english: You asked me recently, brother Fabius, whether one should flee in persecution or not, because something was being announced, though I do not know what. I answered on the spot, as the place and time allowed and as the insistence of certain people demanded, and I carried away with me the subject only half treated. Now I intend to set it out more fully in writing, since your consultation entrusted it to me and the condition of the times had already laid it upon me by its very name. For the more frequent the persecutions that threaten, the more carefully we must examine how faith ought to receive them. And this examination must be undertaken among you, who by not receiving the Comforter, the guide into all truth, are deservedly still struggling with other questions as well.

So I have given your consultation an ordered structure, observing that the first thing to be determined is the status of persecution itself: whether it comes from God or from the devil, so that it may more easily be settled how we ought to meet it. For every matter is clearer once its author is known. It is enough, to be sure, to lay down as a preliminary rule that nothing happens without God's will. But we will not immediately give room to other debates on the basis of this statement, lest we be called away from the present point if someone should answer: "Then evil is from God, and wrongdoing is from God; nothing is left to the devil, nothing even to ourselves." The question now is about persecution. Concerning this, I will say for the moment that nothing happens without God's will, considering that persecution is above all worthy of God and, so to speak, necessary—namely for the testing of his servants or their rejection.

For what is the outcome of persecution, what other effect does it have, except the testing and rejection of faith, by which the Lord will certainly examine his own? Persecution is the Lord's judgment, through which each person is judged either tested or rejected. And judgment belongs to God alone. This is that winnowing fan which even now cleanses the Lord's threshing floor—that is, the church—scattering the confused heap of believers and separating the wheat of martyrs from the chaff of deniers. And this is also the ladder that Jacob dreamed of, showing some an ascent to higher things and others a descent to lower things (Genesis 28:12). So too persecution can be understood as a contest. By whom is the contest proclaimed, except by him by whom the crown and prizes are offered? You read the edict of this contest in Revelation, with what prizes it invites to victory—especially those who have properly conquered in persecution, struggling in victory not against flesh and blood but against spiritual forces of wickedness (Ephesians 6:12). So you will recognize that the decision of the contest belongs to the same contest-president who invites to the prize.

Everything that happens in persecution is for the glory of God, who tests and rejects, who raises up and casts down. And what belongs to the glory of God will certainly come about by his will. But when is God more believed, except when he is more feared—except in the time of persecution? The church is in astonishment. Then faith is more anxious in its expedition and more disciplined in fasts and vigils and prayers and humility, in mutual care and love, in holiness and sobriety. For there is no leisure except for fear and hope. And so from this very fact it is shown to us that what makes God's servants better cannot be attributed to the devil.
orientation: Tertullian opens his treatise by answering Fabius's question whether one should flee in persecution, and begins by establishing that persecution comes from God for the testing of faith.

title: Persecution as God's testing, with the devil only as servant
english: Someone may object: wickedness is not from God but from the devil, and persecution consists of wickedness. For what is more wicked than treating the priests of the true God, all the followers of truth, like the worst criminals? Therefore persecution seems to come from the devil, since the wickedness from which persecution is made is his work. But we must understand this: persecution is not without the devil's wickedness, nor is the testing of faith without persecution. The wickedness necessary for the testing of faith does not give patronage to persecution, but service. God's will concerning the testing of faith comes first; that is the reason for persecution. The devil's wickedness follows as the instrument of persecution, which is the means of testing.

For in other matters too, to the extent that wickedness is the rival of righteousness, it is the material for the testimony of the very thing it rivals, so that righteousness is perfected in wickedness just as strength is perfected in weakness. For God chose the weak things of the world to put the strong to shame, and its foolish things to put wisdom to shame (1 Corinthians 1:27). So wickedness is employed so that righteousness may be tested and put wickedness to shame.

Therefore, since this is not the service of choice but of slavery—for persecution is the choice of the Lord because of the testing of faith, while the devil's wickedness is the service because of the equipping of persecution—we believe that persecution comes through the devil, if at all, not from the devil.

Nothing will be permitted to Satan against the servants of the living God unless the Lord allows it, either to destroy Satan himself through the faith of the elect that conquers in temptation, or to expose as his own those who have fallen away to him. You have the example of Job, on whom the devil could inflict no temptation unless he had received power from God—not even against his property, unless the Lord had said, 'Behold, everything that is his I give into your hand, but do not stretch out your hand against him' (Job 1:12). And indeed he did not stretch out his hand until, when he asked for this too, the Lord said, 'Behold, I hand him over to you, only preserve his life' (Job 2:6).

So also he asked for the power to tempt the apostles, not having it except by permission, since the Lord in the Gospel says to Peter, 'Behold, Satan has asked to sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail' (Luke 22:31-32)—that is, that not so much be permitted to the devil that faith would be endangered. This shows that both things are with God: the assault on faith and its protection, since both are asked from him—the assault by the devil, the protection by the Son. And certainly, since the Son of God has the protection of faith in his own power, which he asks from the Father, from whom he receives all power in heaven and on earth, how could the devil have the assault on faith in his own hand?

But in the appointed prayer, when we say to the Father, 'Lead us not into temptation' (Matthew 6:13)—and what greater temptation is there than persecution?—we confess that it comes from him from whom we pray to be spared it. For this is what follows: 'But deliver us from the evil one' (Matthew 6:13), that is, do not lead us into temptation by permitting us to the evil one. For then we are delivered from the devil's hands when we are not handed over to him in temptation.

Nor did the legion of demons have power over the herd of pigs unless it had obtained it from God; so far is it from having power over God's sheep. I can say that even the bristles of the pigs were numbered before God then, let alone the hairs of the saints. The devil seems to have his own power, if at all, over those who do not belong to God, since the nations were once reckoned by God as a drop of a bucket and the dust of the threshing floor and spittle, and through this were exposed to the devil as an empty possession, so to speak.

But against the household of God nothing is permitted to him from his own power, because when it is permitted—that is, from what causes—the examples marked in the Scriptures demonstrate. For either the right of temptation is granted to him for the cause of testing, whether he is challenged or challenges, as in the cases above; or for the cause of rejection the sinner is handed over to him, as to an executioner for punishment, as with Saul: 'And the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him and choked him' (1 Samuel 16:14). Or for the cause of restraint, as the apostle reports that a thorn was given to him, an angel of Satan, to strike him (2 Corinthians 12:7). Nor is this kind of thing permitted to the devil against the saints, to humble them through bodily affliction, unless at the same time the strength of endurance may be perfected in weakness. For the apostle himself handed over Phygelus and Hermogenes to Satan, so that they might be corrected, lest they blaspheme. You see now that the devil receives power more readily from God's servants; so far is he from possessing it as his own.
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that persecution comes from the devil because it consists in wickedness, and he is explaining how God's will for testing faith precedes and uses the devil's wickedness as a mere instrument.

title: Persecution as God's testing fire
english: Since these examples also occur more in persecutions, since it is then especially that we are tested or rejected, and then especially that we are humbled or corrected, it must be that these things are universally permitted or commanded by the one from whom they come even in part. That is, by the one who says, "I am the one who makes peace and creates evils" (Isaiah 45:7). That is, war, for war is the opposite of peace. And what is persecution but war against our peace? If the outcomes of persecution especially bring either life or death, either wound or healing, you have the author of it: "I will strike and I will heal, I will give life and I will put to death" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "I will burn them," he says, "as gold is burned, and I will test them," he says, "as silver is tested" (Zechariah 13:9). For when we are burned by the heat of persecution, then we are tested in the steadfastness of our faith. These will be the fiery darts of the devil, through which the burning and smelting of faith is carried out, yet by God's will.

Who could doubt this? I do not know, unless it is a plainly frivolous and cold faith that exposes those who gather in the church fearfully. For some of you say, "Because we assemble without order, and we assemble together, and many of us rush into the church, we are sought out by the nations, and we are afraid that the nations will be disturbed." Do you not know that God is Lord of all? And if he is, as it were, God, then you will suffer persecution; but if he does not will it, the nations will be silent. You should certainly believe this, if you believe in that God without whose will not even a sparrow falls to the ground (Matthew 10:29). But we, I think, stand against many sparrows.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that persecution comes from God, and here he applies the biblical examples of testing and humbling to persecution itself, then answers those who fear gathering as a church.

title: Persecution is from God, therefore good and unavoidable
english: So if it is established from whom persecution comes, I can now take up your question and settle it from this very preliminary discussion: there must be no flight in persecution. For if persecution comes from God, then in no way must there be flight from what comes from God. A twofold argument defends this: what comes from God should not be avoided, and it cannot be escaped.

It should not be avoided, because it is good. For everything that has seemed good to God must necessarily be good. And was it not for this reason that Genesis says, "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:10)—not because he would not have known it was good unless he had seen it, but to indicate by this expression that what has seemed good to God is good? Many things, to be sure, come from God and come for someone's harm. No—it is good precisely because it comes from God, as something divine and rational. For what is divine that is not rational, not good? What is good that is not divine?

But if it seems otherwise to anyone's perception, human perception does not prejudge the status of things; rather, the status prejudges perception. For each thing's status is something fixed, and it gives perception the law of perceiving that status as it is. If, then, by status what comes from God is good—for nothing from God is not good, because it is divine, because it is rational—but to perception it seems evil, the status will be secure, and the perception at fault. By status, chastity, truth, and justice are the best things, yet they displease the perception of many. Does that mean the status is made subject to perception? So too persecution is good by status, because it is a divine and rational arrangement, but it displeases the perception of those for whose harm it comes.

You see that even that evil has a rational purpose with God, when someone is overturned from salvation in persecution, just as that good also comes about by reason, when someone advances in salvation through persecution. Unless someone perishes before the Lord or is saved irrationally, he will not be able to call persecution evil, since even in its harmful part it is good, as long as it is administered by reason.

So if persecution is good in whatever way, because it is established by status, we rightly determine that what is good ought not to be avoided, because it is a sin to refuse what is good—all the more so when it has seemed good to God. And further, it cannot be avoided, because it comes from God, whose will cannot be escaped. Therefore those who think there must be flight either reproach God with evil, if they flee persecution as an evil—for no one avoids what is good—or they consider themselves stronger than God, if they think they can escape when God has willed such a thing to come about.
orientation: Tertullian is answering Fabius's question about flight, arguing from the premise just established that persecution comes from God.

title: The logic of flight and God's power
english: Someone objects, "But I am fleeing what belongs to me, so that I do not perish if I deny. It is God's part, if he wills, to bring me back into the midst even as I flee."

First answer me this: are you certain you will deny if you do not flee, or are you uncertain? If you are certain, you have already denied. By presuming you will deny, you have pledged the very thing you presumed, and now you flee in vain to avoid denying. If you are going to deny, you have already denied.

But if you are uncertain, why do you not, from the equal uncertainty of fear between the two outcomes, also presume that you can confess and be saved rather than flee, just as you presume you will deny so that you flee? At this point either both things are in our power or everything is in God's.
If confessing or denying is in our power, why do we not presume what is better, namely that we will confess? Unless you want to confess but do not want to suffer. And refusing to confess is denial.

But if everything is in God's power, why do we not leave everything to his judgment, recognizing his strength and power? Just as he can bring us back into the midst when we flee, so he can shelter us when we do not flee, and even when we are living among the people.

What kind of honor is it to give God credit for your flight, since he can bring you out into the midst even as you flee, but to dishonor him when it comes to bearing witness, despairing of the power of his protection? Why do you not rather say, from this side of steadfastness and trust in God: "I do what is mine to do; I do not leave; God himself will protect me if he wills"? This is more properly ours: to stand under God's judgment than to flee under our own.

Rutilius, that most holy martyr, had fled persecution from place to place so many times, and had even bought his way out of danger with coins, as he thought. After all the security he had arranged for himself, he was unexpectedly seized and handed over to the governor, torn apart by tortures, I believe as chastisement for his flight, and then given to the flames. And so he returned to God's mercy the suffering he had avoided.
What else did the Lord want to show us by this example than that we must not flee, because flight profits nothing if God is unwilling?
orientation: Tertullian is answering Fabius's opening objection that he flees to avoid denying, and now presses him with a dilemma about whether denial is certain or uncertain.

title: The flight command was only for the apostles, for a limited time
english: But, someone says, he fulfilled the command by fleeing from city to city. That is how a certain man wanted to argue, himself also a fugitive, and there are those who refuse to understand the meaning of the Lord's pronouncement so that they can use it as a covering for their own cowardice, even though it had its own persons, times, and reasons.

When they begin to persecute you, he says, flee from city to city (Matthew 10:23). We maintain that this pertains specifically to the persons of the apostles, and to their times and reasons, as the words that follow will prove, since they fit no one but the apostles: Do not go in the way of the nations, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 10:5-6).

But for us the way of the nations lies open. In it we were found, and in it we walk to the end. No city is excluded, since we preach throughout the whole world. Nor has the care of Israel been laid upon us as a special charge, except insofar as we must preach to all nations. Even if we are arrested, we will not be led into their councils or flogged in their synagogues; we will be handed over to Roman authorities and tribunals.

So the condition of the apostles required the command to flee, because the gospel had first to be preached to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. In order that the preaching might be completed among those to whom it had to be completed first, so that the children might take the bread before the dogs, they were commanded to flee at that time. This was not so that they might escape the danger of persecution on their own account. Indeed he foretold that they would suffer persecutions and taught that they must be endured. Rather, it was for the progress of the announcement, so that the dissemination of the gospel might not be destroyed if they were immediately crushed.

For they were not to flee secretly into some city, but as men who would announce the gospel everywhere and therefore undergo persecutions everywhere, until they had filled up their teaching. Finally, he says, You will not finish the cities of Israel (Matthew 10:23). So the command to flee was confined within the borders of Judea.

But for us no boundary of Judea applies to our preaching, since the Holy Spirit has now been poured out upon all flesh. Thus Paul and the apostles themselves, mindful of the Lord's command, testify to Israel, whom they had already filled with their teaching: It was necessary that the word of God be delivered to you first, but since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations (Acts 13:46).

And from then on they turned, as they themselves had previously established, and went into the way of the nations and entered the cities of the Samaritans, so that their sound went out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world (Psalm 19:4). If, then, the exception of the way of the nations and the entrance into the cities of the Samaritans has ceased, why should not the command to flee, which was issued together with it, also have ceased?

Finally, from the time when Israel was filled and the apostles passed over to the nations, they neither fled from city to city nor hesitated to suffer. Indeed Paul, who had let himself be lowered through the wall to escape the persecution that belonged to that time of the command, later, at the close of his ministry and the completion of the command, when the disciples earnestly begged him not to go to Jerusalem to suffer there what Agabus had foretold, did not subscribe to their anxiety.

On the contrary, he said, What are you doing, weeping and troubling my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of my Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 21:13). And so they all said, Let the will of the Lord be done (Acts 21:14).

What was the will of the Lord? Surely no longer to flee persecution. Otherwise they could have set before him the earlier will of the Lord, by which he had commanded flight, those who preferred that he avoid persecution.

Therefore, since even under the apostles themselves the command to flee was temporary, like the rest of their instructions, what ceased among our teachers cannot continue among us, even if it had not been issued specifically to them. Or, if the Lord willed it to continue, the apostles sinned, who did not take care to flee to the end.
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that the Lord's command to flee from city to city still applies to Christians.

title: The Lord's commands contradict a perpetual command to flee
english: Let us now see whether the rest of the Lord's commands agree with a perpetual command to flee. First of all, if persecution comes from God, what sense does it make for the same God who sends it to command that it be fled? If he wanted it to be avoided, he would do better not to send it at all, so that his will would not seem to be violated by another will. For either he wanted us to suffer persecution or to flee. If to flee, how can we suffer? If to suffer, how can we flee? And what a great inconsistency there is between the opinions of one who commands flight and one who invites us to a suffering that is the opposite of flight.

"Whoever confesses me, I will also confess before my Father" (Matthew 10:32). How will he confess while fleeing? How will he flee while confessing? "Whoever has been ashamed of me, I will also be ashamed of him before my Father" (Matthew 10:33). If I avoid suffering, I am ashamed of confession. "Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of my name" (Matthew 5:11). Unblessed, then, are those who by fleeing according to the command will not have suffered. "Whoever endures to the end will be saved" (Matthew 10:22). So why do you command me to flee, yet want me to endure to the end? If such a great diversity of opinions does not agree with divine seriousness, it is clear from these sayings too that the command to flee had its own reason at that time, which we have shown.

But, someone says, the Lord, looking out for the weakness of certain people in his humanity, nevertheless also pointed out a harbor of flight. For he was not able, without flight—such a base, unworthy, and slavish protection—to save in persecution those he knew to be weak.

But he does not cherish the weak; he always rejects them. First he teaches that persecutors are not to be fled, but rather not to be feared. "Do not fear those who can kill the body but can do nothing to the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in hell" (Matthew 10:28). And then what does he prescribe for the cowardly? "Whoever values his own life more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever does not take up his cross and follow me cannot be my disciple" (Matthew 10:37-38; Luke 14:27). Finally, in Revelation he does not offer flight to the cowardly, but among the rest of the rejected ones a share in the lake that burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death (Revelation 21:8).
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that the Lord's own sayings about confession, suffering, and endurance are incompatible with a lasting command to flee persecution.

title: Christ's own example of not fleeing
english: He himself also fled violence sometimes, but for the same reason he had commanded the apostles to flee: until of course he should fulfill his teaching. Once that was completed, I do not say he stood, but he did not even seek help from the Father with armies of angels, after rebuking even Peter's sword. He confessed that his soul was anxious even to death and his flesh weak, to show you first that both human substances were in him—the anxiety of the soul and the weakness of the flesh—so that you would not interpret Christ's flesh or soul as something else, as some have now introduced. Then, having demonstrated their conditions, you would know that they are worth nothing by themselves without the Spirit. And so he puts forward the willing spirit, so that looking at the condition of each substance you may understand that the strength of the Spirit is also in you, just as the weakness of the flesh is, and from this you may know what to do from what and what to subject to what—the weak to the strong—so that you do not, as you now do, complain about the weakness of the flesh while ignoring the firmness of the Spirit. He also asked the Father that, if it were possible, the cup of suffering might pass from him. You too should ask, but standing as he did, asking only, and adding the rest: "Yet not what I will, but what you will". But if you flee, how will you ask this, when you yourself provide the removal of the cup, and do not what the Father wills, but what you will?
orientation: Tertullian is arguing from Christ's own conduct in his passion that flight is not permitted, answering the objection that Christ himself sometimes withdrew.

title: Apostolic teaching and the Spirit forbid flight
english: The apostles certainly taught everything according to God, and unfolded the whole gospel. Where do you show that they restored the command to flee from city to city? They could not have established anything so contrary to their own examples. While they were held in chains or on islands because of their confession, not because of flight from the name, they wrote to the churches.

Paul commands us to support the weak (1 Thessalonians 5:14), and certainly not those who are fleeing. How can the absent be supported? Or is it by patience? He says they are to be supported if they have stumbled through weakness of faith, just as the faint-hearted are to be comforted, but not sent into flight. And when he warns us not to give place to the devil (Ephesians 4:27), he is not suggesting the counsel of flight; he is teaching moderation of anger. And when he says to buy back the time, because the days are evil (Ephesians 5:16), he wants us to gain a reprieve not through flight but through wisdom of conduct.

Besides, the one who commands us to shine as children of light (Ephesians 5:8) does not command us to hide ourselves in flight like children of darkness. He instructs us to stand immovable (Ephesians 6:14), certainly not to be moved by flight, and to be girded. For flight, or for the encounter of the gospel? He also points to weapons that would not be necessary for those about to flee. Among them is the shield, with which you can extinguish the darts of the devil (Ephesians 6:16), resisting without doubt and receiving every assault of his.

So John also teaches that lives are to be laid down for brothers (1 John 3:16), much more for the Lord. This cannot be fulfilled by those who flee. Finally, mindful of his Revelation, in which he had heard the end of the cowardly (Revelation 21:8), he himself warns from his own understanding that fear must be cast out. "Fear," he says, "is not in love. But perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment" (1 John 4:18), certainly the fire of the lake. "Whoever fears is not perfected in love," that is, in the love of God.

But who will flee persecution except the one who fears? Who will fear except the one who has not loved? And if you consult the Spirit, what does the Spirit approve more than that saying? For it exhorts almost everyone to martyrdom, not to flight. Let us remember that saying of the Spirit too: "You are publicly exposed," it says; "it is good for you. For whoever is not made public among men is made public in the Lord. Do not be ashamed; righteousness brings you into the open. Why are you ashamed while bearing praise? Power comes when you are seen by men." So also elsewhere: "Do not wish to depart in beds, or in miscarriages and soft fevers, but in martyrdoms, so that the one who suffered for you may be glorified."
orientation: Tertullian is arguing from the apostles' own teaching and from the Spirit's sayings that flight from persecution was never commanded for Christians.

title: The shame of fleeing God and the example of Jonah
english: But some people set aside the divine exhortations and apply to themselves that Greek little verse of worldly wisdom: "He who fled will fight again"—so that perhaps he may flee again. And when will the one who was defeated by fleeing ever win? A good soldier for Christ his commander is the one who, fully armed by the apostle, hears the trumpet of persecution and deserts the day of persecution. I too will answer with something from the world: Is dying really so miserable? Let a man die one way or another, whether defeated or victor. For even if he falls by denial, he has still fought with torments. I prefer a man to be pitied than to be ashamed. A soldier pierced by a javelin in battle is more honorable than one safe in flight. Do you fear a human being, Christian—you whom angels ought to fear, since you will judge angels; whom demons ought to fear, since you have received power even over demons; whom the whole world ought to fear, since the world is judged in you? You have put on Christ, since you have been dipped into Christ—and you flee from the devil? You have cheapened Christ, who is in you; you have made yourself a fugitive along with the devil. But by fleeing from the Lord you reproach all fugitives for the foolishness of their plan. A certain spirited prophet also fled from the Lord; he had crossed over from Joppa to Tarshish, as if he could sail away from God. But I find him not only in sea and on land, but even in the belly of a beast, where for three days he could neither die nor even so escape God. How much better is the one who, fearing the enemy of God, does not flee from him but rather despises him, trusting in the Lord's protection; or who, fearing God, stands all the more under his eyes, saying: "The Lord is, he is powerful. All things are his; wherever I am, I am in his hand. Let him do what he wills; I do not depart. And if he wishes to destroy me, let him destroy me himself, while I keep myself for him. I prefer to make envy for him by perishing through his will, than to make him angry by escaping through my own."
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that a soldier who flees can fight again, and he now contrasts the shame of flight with the honor of standing before God.

title: Shepherds must not flee when the flock is attacked
english: Every servant of God ought to think and act this way, even one of lower rank, so that he may become greater if he climbs any step in enduring persecution. But when the leaders themselves—the deacons, presbyters, and bishops—flee, how can an ordinary believer understand why it was said, "Flee from city to city" (Matthew 10:23)? So when the commanders flee, who among the common soldiers will hold out to urge that a position be fixed in the battle line? Certainly the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, as Moses—before the Lord Christ was revealed, though already prefigured in him—says: "If you destroy this people," he says, "destroy me as well along with them" (Exodus 32:32). But Christ confirms his own figures: the bad shepherd is the one who sees the wolf and flees, leaving the sheep to be torn apart (John 10:12). Such a shepherd will be thrown out of the estate; the wages of his commission will be withheld as compensation, and restitution for the master's loss will be exacted even from his earlier property. For to the one who has, more will be given, but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away (Matthew 25:29). So Zechariah threatens: "Draw a sword against the shepherds and uproot the sheep, and I will bring my hand upon the shepherds" (Zechariah 13:7, paraphrased). Ezekiel and Jeremiah also speak at length against them with the same threats, because they not only feed improperly on the sheep, pasturing themselves rather than the flock, but also scatter the flock and make it prey for all the beasts of the field, since there is no shepherd for them (Ezekiel 34:2-5). This never happens more than when the church is abandoned by its clergy in persecution. If anyone recognizes the Spirit, he will hear the Spirit denouncing fugitives. Moreover, if those who are set over the flock flee when the wolves rush in, it is not fitting—indeed it is not even lawful. For the one who declared such a shepherd evil certainly condemned him, and everything that is condemned is without doubt made unlawful. Therefore the leaders of the church ought not to flee in persecution. But if the flock ought to flee, the leader of the flock ought not to stand, since he would stand to protect the flock to no purpose—a protection the flock would not want, given its license to flee.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing the duty of church leaders in persecution, arguing that if even the lowest servant must stand, then leaders who flee leave the flock without a shepherd.

title: Buying one's way out is flight and dishonors Christ's blood
english: As for your question, brother, you now have my answer and my urging. But anyone who asks whether persecution should be fled must also look ahead to the next question: if it should not be fled, should one at least buy one's way out? So I will go further and offer you my view on this too. I hold that persecution, which we have established should not be fled, should likewise not be bought off. The price is the only difference. Just as flight is a free buying of one's way out, so money buying of one's way out is flight. Certainly it is also a counsel of cowardice. You buy off what you fear, therefore you flee. You stood your ground with your feet, but you ran with your money. By the very fact that you stood, you fled through buying your way out. But for you to buy a man with money whom Christ bought with his own blood—how unworthy of God and his purposes! He did not spare his own Son for you, so that he became a curse for us, because cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree (Galatians 3:13). He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7); he gave his back to the whips and his cheeks to blows, and did not turn his face away from spitting (Isaiah 50:6); he was numbered among the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12) and handed over to death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). All this, to gain us from our sins. The sun withdrew from the day of our purchase. Our re-purchase was transacted among the dead, and our contract is in heaven. The eternal gates were lifted up so that the King of glory, the Lord of hosts, might enter (Psalm 24:7), having bought humanity from the earth—no, from the dead—into heaven. Who is there now who struggles against him, or rather cheapens his merchandise, bought at so great a price—the most precious blood—and defiles it? Better to flee than to become cheaper, if a man will not cost himself as much as he cost the Lord. And the Lord indeed bought him back from the angels who hold sway over the world, from spiritual forces of wickedness, from the darkness of this age, from eternal judgment, from perpetual death. But you bargain for him with an informer or a soldier or some petty thief of a governor, under your tunic and in your pocket, as they say, as if by stealth—as if he were stolen goods, the man whom Christ bought openly before the whole world, and indeed set free. Will you put a price on this free man and possess him for a price, unless it is the same price he cost the Lord, as we said—his own blood? Why then do you ransom Christ from a man, in the man in whom Christ is? Simon tried to do the same thing when he offered the apostles money for the Spirit of Christ. So let this man too, who by buying himself out bought out the Spirit of Christ, hear: May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money (Acts 8:20). Who would despise a denier? What does that extortionist say? Give me money. At least so that he will not hand you over, since he is selling nothing other than what he will deliver in return for your payment. When you give, you certainly wanted not to be handed over. But if you were not handed over, would you have been publicly exposed? So while, by refusing to be handed over, you refuse to be exposed, by that refusal you have denied what you refused to be exposed as. 'No,' you say, 'by refusing to be exposed as what I am, I have confessed that I am what I refuse to be exposed as, that is, a Christian.' Can Christ then claim you as a martyr for having shown yourself steadfastly? Buying your way out does not show it. You confessed before one person, perhaps; therefore by not wanting to confess before many, you denied. Salvation itself will judge that a man has fallen while he escapes. He has fallen, then, who preferred to have escaped. Refusing martyrdom is also denial. A Christian is saved by money, and he keeps coins for this purpose—so that he will not suffer, as long as he is rich against God. But Christ was rich in blood for him. Blessed are the poor, then, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:3)—those who have only their soul in their possession. If we cannot serve God and money (Matthew 6:24), can we be bought back both by God and by money? For who will serve money more than the man whom money has bought back? Finally, what example do you use for buying your way out of betrayal? When the apostles were driven about by persecutions, when did they free themselves with money? They certainly did not lack it, since the prices of lands were laid at their feet, and there were many wealthy believing men and women who supplied them with refreshment. When did Onesiphorus or Aquila or Stephen help them in persecution in this way? As for Paul, when Felix the governor hoped to receive money from the disciples for him—and he discussed this privately with Paul himself—neither Paul for himself nor the disciples for him paid anything. Those disciples, weeping because he still insisted on going to Jerusalem and did not avoid the persecutions foretold there, finally said: Let the will of God be done (Acts 21:14). What was that will? Surely that he should suffer for the name of the Lord, not that he should be bought off. For just as Christ laid down his life for us, so it must be done for him by us—and not only for him, but even for the brothers for his sake. John taught this when he declared that we should not buy back the brothers, but rather die for them (1 John 3:16). It makes no difference whether you should not buy a Christian or should not purchase one. And so the will of God is this. Look at the state of kingdoms and empires, surely arranged by God, in whose hand is the heart of the king. Every day so many remedies are devised for increasing the treasury—censuses, taxes, contributions, tributes—and never up to now has anything of this kind been devised against Christians, to reduce them under some buying one's way out for their lives and their sect, although from so great a multitude, known to everyone, an enormous profit could be reaped. Bought with blood, paid for with blood, we owe no coin for our head, because our head is Christ. It is not fitting for Christ to cost money. How could martyrdoms happen for the glory of the Lord if we compensated for the sect's license with a payment? Therefore the man who bargains for it with a price opposes the divine purpose. Since Caesar has imposed nothing on us in the way of a tribute-paying sect—nor could he ever impose such a thing, with the antichrist already pressing in and gaping for the blood, not the money, of Christians—how can anyone propose to me the Scripture, Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's (Matthew 22:21)? A soldier or an informer or an enemy shakes me down, demanding nothing for Caesar—indeed acting against Caesar—when he lets a Christian, guilty under human laws, go for a fee. The denarius I owe Caesar is another matter, one that belongs to him, the tribute that was then under discussion—owed by tribute-payers, not by free men. Or how shall I render to God the things that are God's—that is, his image and coinage inscribed with his name, the Christian man? What do I owe God, as I owe Caesar a denarius, except the blood that his Son poured out for me? But if I owe God my humanity and my blood, and I am now in the time when what I owe God is being demanded, then surely I defraud God by acting to avoid paying what I owe. I have kept the command well—rendering to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, but denying to God the things that are God's.
orientation: Tertullian has just concluded that church leaders must not flee in persecution, and now he turns to the related question of whether a Christian may pay money to escape being handed over.

title: Giving, not extortion; mammon-friends and the shame of taxed churches
english: But I will give to everyone who asks me when the cause is almsgiving, not extortion. "To the one who asks," he says (Matthew 5:42). But the extortionist does not ask. The one who threatens, if he does not receive, does not request; he wrings it out. The man who comes not to be pitied but to be feared is not looking for almsgiving. So I will give in the name of mercy, not of my own cowardice, where the one who receives honors God and returns a blessing to me, not where he thinks he has done me an even greater favor and, looking at his booty, says, "Consider this your payment for guilt."

Will I be angry even at an enemy? But enmities have other grounds as well. Yet he did not say "the betrayer" or "the persecutor" or "the extortionist." For how much more will I heap coals on his head if I do not buy my way out (Romans 12:20)? "Therefore," he says, "if someone takes your tunic, give him your cloak as well" (Matthew 5:40). That applies to the one who tries to take my property, not my faith. I will give my cloak too, but not to the one threatening betrayal. If he threatens, I will demand my tunic back.

All the Lord's sayings now have their own occasions and rules. Their boundaries do not extend infinitely or apply to everything. And indeed he commands giving to everyone who asks, yet he himself does not give a sign to those who ask. Otherwise, if you think we must give to everyone who asks indiscriminately, you seem to me ready to give, I will not say wine to a feverish man, but even poison or a sword to one who desires death.

"Make friends for yourselves by means of money" (Luke 16:9). Let the parable that comes before it teach you how this should be understood. It was spoken to the Jewish people, who had badly administered the stewardship entrusted to them. They ought to provide for themselves friends rather than enemies from among the people of money, that is, from us, and they ought to relieve us of the debts of sins by which we were held bound to God, if they would grant us this according to the Lord's accounting. Then, when grace began to fail them, they might flee to our faith and be received into eternal dwellings.

For now, suppose some other interpretation of that parable and saying, as long as you know it is not likely that our extortionists, brought into friendship through money, will then receive us into eternal dwellings. But what will cowardice not persuade? As if Scripture permits flight and commands buying one's way out.

Finally, it is not enough if one or another is rescued in this way. Whole churches have imposed a tax on themselves en masse. I do not know whether to grieve or blush when Christians are listed as taxpayers in the registers of the police-soldiers and informers, among tavern-keepers and doorkeepers and bathhouse thieves and gamblers and pimps. Did the apostles establish this pattern for the episcopate with such foresight, so that they could enjoy their rule in security under the pretext of administration? Surely this is the peace Christ commanded when he returned to the Father, to be bought from soldiers during the Saturnalia!
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that Christians may pay their way out of persecution, and he now distinguishes true almsgiving from paying extortionists, then turns to the parable of the unjust steward and the shame of churches paying tribute.

title: Faith and wisdom, not money, protect; the Spirit enables endurance
english: But how shall we gather, you say? How shall we celebrate the Lord's solemn rites? Surely the way the apostles did: safe by faith, not by money. If faith can move a mountain (Matthew 17:20), it can move a soldier far more easily. Be cautious by wisdom, not by a bribe. You will not be safe from the people just because you have bought off the military services. You need faith and wisdom together for your protection. Without them, you can lose even the buying of your way out; with them, you have no need of it.

Finally, if you cannot gather by day, you have the night, with the light of Christ shining against it. You cannot run around to each one? Let the church be for you also among three. It is better not to see your crowds sometimes than to betray them. Keep for Christ the virgin bride; let no one make a profit from her.

These things, brother, perhaps seem hard and intolerable to you. But remember that God said, "Let the one who can receive it receive it" (Matthew 19:12). That is, let the one who cannot receive it depart. The one who fears to suffer cannot belong to the one who suffered. But the one who does not fear to suffer will be made perfect in love, the love of God. For perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18). And therefore many are called, but few are chosen (Matthew 22:14). The question is not who is ready to follow the wide road, but who is ready for the narrow one (Matthew 7:13-14).

And therefore the Comforter is necessary, the guide into all truth, the exhorter of all endurances. Those who have received him have known neither how to flee persecution nor how to buy their way out, since they have the one who will be for us. As he will speak in our interrogation, so he will help in our suffering.
orientation: Tertullian is answering the practical objection that Christians must gather and celebrate the Lord's rites, explaining that faith and wisdom, not money, are the true protection, and that those who have received the Comforter will neither flee nor buy their way out.
